## CHAPTER III HIGH-RISK AI SYSTEMS

## SECTION 1 Classification of AI systems as high-risk

## Article 6 Classification rules for high-risk AI systems

1. Irrespective of whether an AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the products referred to in points (a) and (b), that AI system shall be considered to be high-risk where both of the following conditions are fulfilled:

(a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I;

(b) the product whose safety component pursuant to point (a) is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, with a view to the placing on the market or the putting into service of that product pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I.

2. In addition to the high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1, AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk.

3. By derogation from paragraph 2, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall not be considered to be high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making.

The first subparagraph shall apply where any of the following conditions is fulfilled:

(a) the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task;

(b) the AI system is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity;

(c) the AI system is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review; or

Notwithstanding the first subparagraph, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons.

4. A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk shall document its assessment before that system is placed on the market or put into service. Such provider shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2). (61) Certain AI systems intended for the administration of justice and democratic processes should be classified as high-risk, considering their potentially significant impact on democracy, the rule of law, individual freedoms as well as the right to an effective remedy and to a fair trial. In particular, to address the risks of potential biases, errors and opacity, it is appropriate to qualify as high-risk AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority or on its behalf to assist judicial authorities in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts. AI systems intended to be used by alternative dispute resolution bodies for those purposes should also be considered to be high-risk when the outcomes of the alternative dispute resolution proceedings produce legal effects for the parties. The use of AI tools can support the decision-making power of judges or judicial independence, but should not replace it: the final decision-making must remain a human-driven activity. The classification of AI systems as high-risk should not, however, extend to AI systems intended for purely ancillary administrative activities that do not affect the actual administration of justice in individual cases, such as anonymisation or pseudonymisation of judicial decisions, documents or data, communication between personnel, administrative tasks.

(62) Without prejudice to the rules provided for in Regulation (EU) 2024/900 of the European Parliament and of the Council (34), and in order to address the risks of undue external interference with the right to vote enshrined in Article 39 of the Charter, and of adverse effects on democracy and the rule of law, AI systems intended to be used to influence the outcome of an election or referendum or the voting behaviour of natural persons in the exercise of their vote in elections or referenda should be classified as high-risk AI systems with the exception of AI systems whose output natural persons are not directly exposed to, such as tools used to organise, optimise and structure political campaigns from an administrative and logistical point of view.

(63) The fact that an AI system is classified as a high-risk AI system under this Regulation should not be interpreted as indicating that the use of the system is lawful under other acts of Union law or under national law compatible with Union law, such as on the protection of personal data, on the use of polygraphs and similar tools or other systems to detect the emotional state of natural persons. Any such use should continue to occur solely in accordance with the applicable requirements resulting from the Charter and from the applicable acts of secondary Union law and national law. This Regulation should not be understood as providing for the legal ground for processing of personal data, including special categories of personal data, where relevant, unless it is specifically otherwise provided for in this Regulation.

(64) To mitigate the risks from high-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service and to ensure a high level of trustworthiness, certain mandatory requirements should apply to high-risk AI systems, taking into account the intended purpose and the context of use of the AI system and according to the risk-management system to be established by the provider. #### 1.1.A. The ChatGPT turning point

Historians may look back on November 30, 2022, as the critical turning point in the development of generative Al. Although beforehand, the technology was in widespread use, particularly in academia, it was on that date that OpenAI released ChatGPT to the world. When it did so, it shot the starting gun for what has turned into an "Al arms race,"1 in which technology companies now compete to develop the most sophisticated models as quickly as possible.2 In March 2023, four months following the release of ChatGPT in November 2022, OpenAl launched GPT-4, a model with dramatically enhanced capabilities. Concurrently, Anthropic introduced Claude, a direct competitor to GPT-4.3 Meta unveiled its open model, Llama 2, in July 2023, Mistral Al released Mistral 7B in September 2023, Baidu launched Ernie 4.0 one month later, followed by X.ai's release of Grok in November and Google's release of Gemini at the close of 2023. The momentum continued into 2024, with Anthropic releasing Claude 3 in March, Meta introducing Llama 3 in April, and OpenAI releasing GPT-40 in May.

At present, only a select few Al companies, often global tech giants, possess the expertise and financial resources necessary to develop the most advanced generative Al systems and models (see section 2.2.5.). Having invested in Al for many years, these leading Al companies are well-positioned to dominate the burgeoning generative Al market. Yet small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), startups, researchers, and open-source developers are also playing a role in the generative Al ecosystem.

In particular, while most leading Al companies opt to keep the proprietary details of their Al systems private, an increasing number of developers are choosing to be open.4 The presence of these open models facilitates a potentially competitive market that distinguishes this technological ecosystem from the monopolistic tendencies of recent technological advancements, for example, in social media and search engines. At the same time, the openness of the models necessarily presents unique risks, as the model developers cannot foresee or rein in the efforts of bad actors who might use these models to create harm (see section 3.2.6.A.).

Competition in Al is not limited to companies, of course: It extends to nation states. Because of the potential power of this new technology, let alone its military and intelligence applications, the Al arms race has similarities to an actual arms race, as countries compete to develop offensive and defensive capabilities to promote national interests. The Al revolution, therefore, has far-reaching geopolitical implications. In the words of a Brookings Institution 2020 blog post: "Whoever leads in artificial intelligence in 2030 will rule the world until 2100."5

Determining the model's size mainly involves determining the number of parameters163 or weights it will include. "Weights" are the numerical values that determine the strength of neural connections within a neural network and, thereby, help determine a model's output. During the training process, these weights are adjusted to optimize the model's performance, helping it produce more accurate and useful outputs. Furthermore, the relationship between the size of the model and its performance is mediated by the model's topology. "Topology" refers to the arrangement of neurons and layers within the neural network and how they are interconnected. It determines how input data are processed and how different features are extracted and combined to generate outputs. A dramatic increase in the size (number of parameters) of generative AI models has been a key driver of recently improved capabilities. In 2018, GPT used only 117 million parameters and, in 2019, GPT-2 had 1.5 billion parameters.164 But in 2020, OpenAI pioneered advancements in the field with the introduction of GPT-3, a cutting-edge language model at the time, boasting 175 billion parameters. 165 The size of GPT-4 (2023) has not been officially released, but it is believed to be significantly larger, with estimates suggesting up to 1 trillion parameters. Generative Al offers the potential to revolutionize multiple sectors-education, entertainment, healthcare, and scientific research-by enabling the creation of customized, scalable content, automating processes, generating hypotheses, and boosting efficiency. In software development, generative Al accelerates the coding process by generating code snippets and analyzing existing code to suggest optimizations. It also enhances data analysis, producing synthetic data that can be used to train models when real data are scarce or sensitive. Generative Al supports scientific research by generating hypotheses and simulating experiments, saving time and resources. In healthcare, it can assist in drug discovery and the development of personalized treatment plans by simulating complex biological processes. Finally, generative Al can aid in the detection and prevention of fraud by generating realistic scenarios that help identify vulnerabilities in security systems.

Some characterize the opportunities offered by generative Al as extraordinary, with the expectation that the technology will lead to significant scientific breakthroughs, economic growth, and profound social transformations. The most extreme pronouncement of the utopian vision of Al comes from Marc Andreessen's Techno-Optimist Manifesto: "We believe technology is liberatory. Liberatory of human potential. Liberatory of the human soul, the human spirit. Expanding what it can mean to be free, to be fulfilled, to be alive. We believe technology opens the space of what it can mean to be human."11 In July 2023, the British Computer Society (BCS) appeared to agree with this approving

assessment. The BCS released an open letter calling for the UK government and industry to recognize Al as "a transformational force for good, not an existential threat to humanity."12 The letter attracted over 1,300 signatures.

#### 1.1.C. Fears and worries: a pause

Since the release of ChatGPT, the excitement surrounding generative Al has been modulated by concerns the technology -open or closed source- has raised. In OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's words, "if this technology goes wrong, it can go quite wrong."13 Many worry that Al companies, in their rush to innovate, may overlook the importance of ensuring their models are safe and aligned with human values. This anxiety led numerous researchers and industry leaders, such as Elon Musk and Steve Wozniak, to sign an open letter14 in March 2023, calling on "all Al labs to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of Al systems more powerful than GPT-4." Endorsed by over 33,000 signatories, the letter urged that stakeholders slow down, if not stop, the technological race. One signatory said the letter was provoked, at least in part, by an alleged "corporate irresponsibility,"15 presumably referring to a lack of self-regulation by major Al companies.

## · And mitigating AI risks is a true challenge in business adoption

Hallucination, bias, confidentiality: these are the risks and limits that are holding companies back from using AI, through a healthy respect for both the regulatory framework, and a context where the acceptable margin of error in decision-making is low. So what do we mean by this?

· Hallucination: generative Als are based on a multitude of documents. When the next word to predict matches the truth, all is well. But otherwise? They must choose one option, and can hallucinate untruths with great aplomb. Users therefore need to be trained to use these AIs properly, and to verify every single claim they make.

. Bias: they are rarely intentional, but algorithmic biases are based on data reflecting human practice. The system can therefore discriminate against a specific group of people. A major obstacle for businesses is to identify potential biases (lack of qualified data), raise awareness among employees and have the resources to do so (a dedicated inclusive team, for instance, or a taxonomy programmed with contextual information), and then deal with the biases.

. Privacy: The confidentiality rules of GenAl, and ChatGPT in particular, are still poorly understood. Bear in mind that any data and/or code sent to one of these platforms is likely to be used for subsequent training, which raises issues of confidentiality of corporate data (or that of its customers) and intellectual property.

Overcoming these risks is not an option, it's a sine qua non condition for some businesses. However, the adoption of AI itself is facilitated when it is designed responsibly from the outset: ethical standards reinforce confidence in its use; responsible practices in critical sectors such as human resources guarantee a positive and equitable societal impact; operational excellence prevents abuse and ensures that the AI is beneficial and reliable... Adopting a responsible AI is thus becoming a crucial approach to minimizing risk.

## . Key Issue

### How do we turn this AI revolution into a competitive advantage?

We need new "software" to tackle this profound change in the way we work, and even in the way we do business. New responsible governance must overcome all the risks generated by the use of AI and generative AI. By evolving into an "AI-ready" business, organizations put in place the conditions that will enable them to meet the key business challenges of the future, and perpetuate their business practices and even their business model. It's a moment of truth for organizations: yes, there is a turning point ahead; yet it does not have to be a problem: by implementing a "responsible-by-design" approach, organizations are better equipped to deal with the risks -not just compliance risks, but also business risks- created by the exploding use of Al (see pillars).

Ekimetrics intends to accompany this revolution with a simple, easy-to-understand framework to support these organizations in their AI transformation and the use of these technologies. We have therefore developed 7 pillars of responsible AI, designed to create this competitive edge (see next chapter).

### GenAIs are expanding into the world of business...

... to win the race against time, cumbersome tasks such as taking minutes at meetings, writing e-mails and summarizing documents can now be performed by generative AIs like ChatGPT. Corollary: employees can refocus their productivity on higher value-added tasks.

Banking4, finance, media, NGOs, ESG players: some sectors are pioneers in the use of these new technologies. In fact, Ekimetrics has already been asked to implement:

. Question answering and sourcing: with their ability to search for information in massive databases, new-generation AIs produce immediate answers to business questions, and can isolate specific criteria (a selection of CVs for HR; or in healthcare, in diagnosis tools or looking up information in research literature, for example). The demand for transparency, explainability and security is driving companies to implement a kind of internal ChatGPT, enabling them to track the source of the information they need. # Responsible AI: A competitive edge in the data and GenAI landscape

How Responsible Al enables the use of data, Al, and Gen Al technologies to create a strategic business advantage

<!-- PageBreak -->

<!-- PageHeader: Ekimetrics. -->

## Introduction

### Understand how and why AI makes a decision...

You have probably already applied for a loan from a bank. You have submitted your application for review by your account manager. Income, account management, personal situation, residual savings, downpayment: did you know that all these loan approval criteria are already analyzed by algorithms and artificial intelligence (AI)? Objective criteria? Are you sure?! How can you prove that you have not been discriminated against due to a black box effect? So what is a black box effect? It's a bit like trying to study a car engine without being able to open the hood. You input data into the box -the Al, a Machine Learning system for example- and results are output, which may be remarkable ... yet you're unable to explain the process that allowed the algorithm to make its choices. Understanding the reasons behind the decisions made by an algorithm is essential to ensure its accuracy and avoid bias (often the same discriminations as in the "real world", linked to gender, age, skin color or nationality1). In other words, the aim is to guarantee equal rights, whether for securing a loan, access to public services, hiring ...

### ... and make it strategic

And here's when we need to talk about responsible Al. Let's say that in our first example, you're no longer the one applying for the loan. You're the one who manages the bank or the IT system or the analytics. And for you, "Responsible AI" means "yet more new regulations, more rules to change and implement!". But if we tell you that responsible AI will help you optimize your costs, beef up your customer service or even your loyalty/satisfaction strategy, and easily maintain your platforms while complying with regulations, perhaps you'll see it as a major opportunity to build future-proof practices and business models. Let's rephrase: responsible AI does not have to be synonymous with constraints and compliance. On the contrary: because it is responsible, this approach to AI creates value and gives companies a true competitive edge.

Responsible AI is all the more critical now that generative AIs (see below) have entered with a bang into all strata of society. The biases remain the same as those of the "old" AI. But their effects have multiplied: using colossal volumes of data2 , these "GenAI" generate new data, which is in turn used as input for decision-making. How can we trust them, and guarantee that an organization's products and services are reliable? Responsible AI is therefore becoming a cornerstone of business strategy. And we're not talking here about 5, 10 or 15-year business strategies. We're talking about what can be implemented now, with today's know-how and knowledge. This white paper is a practical guide to responsible AI for business.

##### 3.3.1.B. Privacy concerns

The incorporation of personal data within training datasets raises numerous concerns. The primary issue is that personal data may be incorporated without the knowledge or consent of the individuals concerned, even though the data may include names, identification numbers, Social Security numbers, or other personal information.

Another particularly difficult problem is related to the fact that complex models may "memorize" (i.e., store) specific threads of training data and regurgitate them when responding to a prompt.498 This data memorization can directly lead to leakage of personal data.499 The risk

appears to get worse as both the size of the models and their training sets increase.500 In practice, jailbreaks have proven able to bypass security measures. These included code segments, passages of text, and potentially sensitive personal information, such as names, email addresses, and phone numbers. ## Le plan d'action sur l'IA de l'autorité de protection des données française

En mai 2023, la CNIL a publié son plan d'action [66] relatif aux systèmes d'IA. Elle y indique plusieurs axes de travaux prioritaires visant à appréhender leur fonctionnement et leur impact sur les personnes :

· Loyauté et transparence : cela comprend notamment l'information mise à disposition des personnes dont les données personnelles sont traitées via des systèmes d'IA;

· Protection des données publiquement accessibles : il s'agit des données personnelles et publiquement accessibles (par exemple sur les réseaux sociaux) utilisées pour entraîner les modèles ;

· Protection des données transmises par les utilisateurs : en considérant l'exemple des agents conversationnels, il s'agit des textes rédigés par les utilisateurs des agents. Ces textes peuvent être collectés et partagés à des tiers, notamment afin d'améliorer les modèles. Dans leurs interactions avec les agents conversationnels, les utilisateurs peuvent partager des données personnelles hautement sensibles, telles que des questions relatives à la gestion de leur santé mentale (671. Cela a amené des sociétés à interdire l'utilisation d'agents conversationnels externes de peur de voir leurs données confidentielles être divulguées accidentellement ou via de l'espionnage industriel [68] ;

· Conséquences sur les droits des personnes concernées : il s'agit, par exemple, du droit de rectification évoqué précédemment. Un professeur de droit états- unien était cité - à tort - par ChatGPT lorsque le système était interrogé sur les universitaires ayant sexuellement harcelé quelqu'un [69] ;

· Protection contre les biais et les discriminations ;

· Enjeux de sécurité : il s'agit de nouveaux enjeux à l'intersection entre la sécurité et les données personnelles, comme les clones de voix utilisés à des fins malveillantes (70]. · encadrer le développement de systèmes d'IA respectueux des données personnelles via des publications et une consultation publique à venir sur le partage et la réutilisation des données ;

· accompagner des acteurs innovants de l'écosystème européen et français ;

## · Responsible AI for dummies

### The issue of impact.

Previously, Al was often a matter for specialists - data, sales, marketing, IT, etc. Today, although not everyone works with Machine Learning, anyone can use ChatGPT. In fact, it took this technology just 5 days to pass the million-user mark, and two months to reach 100,000 million.

This democratization of AI use therefore represents a major turning point: HR, the justice system, public services, etc .: all spheres of society now benefit from it -sometimes with proven and critical societal impacts (see diagram). This democratization requires increased attention to excellence in AI implementation, with stronger monitoring and equal rights protection. Safeguards must therefore be implemented from both a technical and a human standpoint, taking risks into account and correcting them as best we can.

## WHAT ARE BIASES AND WHY ARE THEY DANGEROUS?

Social bias broadly encompasses disparate treatment or outcomes between social groups, arising from historical and structural power asymmetries. In the context of Natural Language Processing (NLP), this entails representational harms (misrepresentation, stereotyping, unequal system performance, derogatory language, and exclusionary norms) and allocative harms (direct discrimination and indirect discrimination).

Discrimination is the unjust or prejudicial treatment of different categories of people, especially on the grounds of ethnicity, age, sex, or disability.

A protected attribute is the shared identity trait that determines the group identity of a social group (gender, age, ethnicity, etc.).

It's the democratization mentioned earlier that's forcing them to rethink their approach, often to comply with regulations or to avoid losing a competitive edge by remaining in a situation that puts their business at risk.

## 3· Interpretability pillar

### Core concept

Ensure access to the factors (characteristics and/or variables) that determine a model's decisions and/or predictions

### What are the risks?

· For your business customers > inability to explain model decisions/predictions. Example: what factors enable an algorithm to establish a medical diagnosis? Or refuse a loan?

· For your end customers > discrimination, prejudice against the legal right to know the factors leading to the decision/prediction (black box effect).

· For your organization > loss of control over your model (black box effect), legal and compliance risks, business risks

Where do you start? For directly interpretable algorithms:

V Use simple regressions and decision trees

For algorithms that are not directly interpretable:

V Add control libraries or algorithmic layers to determine how the model works (Lime and Shape are frequently used tools)

What's the competitive advantage?

· For your customers > trust

· For your organization > control your system, compliance, rigorous customer service (= giving objective reasons to end customers)

## WHAT IS A "BLACK BOX EFFECT"?

It's the inability to explain how an algorithmic model makes its decisions. In other words, it's providing the link between the initial data and the final decision.

## DIRECTLY, NOT DIRECTLY INTERPRETABLE: WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE?

There are 3 types of directly interpretable algorithm: linear regression, logistic regression and the simple decision tree. This type of algorithm provides direct access to a model's characteristics.

Other algorithms are not directly interpretable: this is the case for most of the models used: set models, SVMs, artificial neural networks, etc. In these cases, additional toolboxes are needed to access the interpretability of the model and prediction.

## C.4. The ensemble complexity

It is important to note that combining directly interpretable models (weak learners) induces the loss of the interpretability. For example, tree-based ensemble models by bagging (random forest) or boosting (adaboost, gradient boosting, XGboost) are not directly interpretable even if based on simple decision trees, as each tree only sees a subpart of the data and that their outputs are combined.

Stacking models also makes the system non-directly interpretable, even if, once again, every stacked models are simple models.

## C.5. Performance/Interpretability Trade-off

Often, more complex models give better performance. Especially for complex datasets, XGBoost for example will perform better than a simple decision tree. But that added complexity leads to the loss of the interpretability. We talk about the Performance / Interpretability Trade-off.

Source: figure from Arrieta et al. 2019 that you can find here: Re (PDF) Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): Concepts, Taxonomies, Opportunities and Challenges toward Responsible AI

We highly recommend reading this paper for more information on the subject.

There is no general guideline to follow to resolve this trade-off, it is a case-by-case consideration to make. Depending on the risk/criticality for the users of the model you are building and the regulation in place, you might not have a choice to go for a directly interpretable algorithm. In the other cases, it is always better to start simple and to increase the complexity until reaching a satisfying level of performance.

<!-- PageBreak -->

# D. Toolboxes for indirect interpretability

There are many tools to 'open the black box' and get information about the model, but keep in mind that there are all indirect variable estimations and are just indications and certainly not exact information.

Most of these techniques are universal (model agnostic) and can be applied to all algorithms/models. However, certain tools are better suited for certain types of data and certain type of models. We will mainly focus on two toolboxes: Lime and SHAP as there are the ones most widely used.

## D.1. Structured data

For structured data, and for models that are not directly interpretable, we suggest the use of these two toolboxes, LIME and Shap.

Document: Standards - Interpretability

# 3- Interpretability

Machine Learning changed the way computer programs are done. Developers used to formalize a problem and code the rules that would transform input data into output data. Now, it is the model that determines the rules that link the input and output data through iterations and error minimization. It is this ability that gives all its power to Machine Learning and allows us to solve problems that exceed human formalization capabilities. But it is also coupled with a constraint: the rules applied by the model after training to make its predictions and decision may evade human control. For certain types of models, these rules sometimes remain unknown, even if interpretability techniques have made great progress in recent years. This is the famous "black box effect". However, when we decide to use Al to make decisions or make predictions that will have an impact on the lives of citizens, it is crucial, and soon to be regulatory, to keep control of the models and guarantee their explicability.

The interpretability of AI models is therefore becoming a major challenge, both for those who design them and for those who use them. It is a question of knowing which factors influence each decision and prediction (local interpretability) but also which rules govern the model in general (global interpretability).

Interpretability can be defined as having access to the features or variables that are driving the decisions or predictions of a model.

An Interpretable system becomes:

· Explicable: we can provide information and explanation (see the Explicability section)

· Transparent: it has a functioning intelligible to a human

· Provable: it can provide proof of the accuracy of the result

Whatever your use-case, it is critical to use interpretability methods.

If your system is critical, you should use directly interpretable models (regressions or simple decision trees), you can refer to Section 3.C.Direct Interpretability for more information.

If you are not required Direct Interpretability, are decided to use more complex models, you can use toolboxes to access indirect interpretability. You can refer to Section 3.D for more information, depending on the type of data (tabular, text or images).

## A. For whom?

<!-- PageBreak -->

### A.1. The regulator

As mentioned in the section about legal risks in Introduction, the new European law on AI will describe different levels of criticality for AI models. Depending on the level, complete or partial interpretability will be asked by law and in addition to documentation, some audits might occur. Therefore, interpretability will become mandatory for many AI models.

### A.2. The developer or Data Scientist

The data scientist needs to access, as best as possible, the parameters of a model to understand it, to fix possible mistakes, to improve its performance and to stay in control.

#### A.3. The main user

The user needs information in order to best use the product or solution as well as to trust its recommendation. Adoption is driven by trust and very linked to the information that will be provided. We will get into more details about that in the Explicability section of these Guidelines.

#### A.4. The final user

The final user is the person who is the subject of the prediction or decision. That can be the same person as the main user or a different one. For example, we can have a skin diagnostic solution for doctors (main users) that concerns their patients (final users). This group of people may ask for information about the decision/prediction of the algorithm and in many case, they have the legal right to know what were the factor that lead to the decision/prediction.

## · And mitigating AI risks is a true challenge in business adoption

Hallucination, bias, confidentiality: these are the risks and limits that are holding companies back from using AI, through a healthy respect for both the regulatory framework, and a context where the acceptable margin of error in decision-making is low. So what do we mean by this?

· Hallucination: generative Als are based on a multitude of documents. When the next word to predict matches the truth, all is well. But otherwise? They must choose one option, and can hallucinate untruths with great aplomb. Users therefore need to be trained to use these AIs properly, and to verify every single claim they make.

. Bias: they are rarely intentional, but algorithmic biases are based on data reflecting human practice. The system can therefore discriminate against a specific group of people. A major obstacle for businesses is to identify potential biases (lack of qualified data), raise awareness among employees and have the resources to do so (a dedicated inclusive team, for instance, or a taxonomy programmed with contextual information), and then deal with the biases.

. Privacy: The confidentiality rules of GenAl, and ChatGPT in particular, are still poorly understood. Bear in mind that any data and/or code sent to one of these platforms is likely to be used for subsequent training, which raises issues of confidentiality of corporate data (or that of its customers) and intellectual property.

Overcoming these risks is not an option, it's a sine qua non condition for some businesses. However, the adoption of AI itself is facilitated when it is designed responsibly from the outset: ethical standards reinforce confidence in its use; responsible practices in critical sectors such as human resources guarantee a positive and equitable societal impact; operational excellence prevents abuse and ensures that the AI is beneficial and reliable... Adopting a responsible AI is thus becoming a crucial approach to minimizing risk.

# Responsible AI: A competitive edge in the data and GenAI landscape

How Responsible Al enables the use of data, Al, and Gen Al technologies to create a strategic business advantage

<!-- PageBreak -->

## Introduction

### Understand how and why AI makes a decision...

You have probably already applied for a loan from a bank. You have submitted your application for review by your account manager. Income, account management, personal situation, residual savings, downpayment: did you know that all these loan approval criteria are already analyzed by algorithms and artificial intelligence (AI)? Objective criteria? Are you sure?! How can you prove that you have not been discriminated against due to a black box effect? So what is a black box effect? It's a bit like trying to study a car engine without being able to open the hood. You input data into the box -the Al, a Machine Learning system for example- and results are output, which may be remarkable ... yet you're unable to explain the process that allowed the algorithm to make its choices. Understanding the reasons behind the decisions made by an algorithm is essential to ensure its accuracy and avoid bias (often the same discriminations as in the "real world", linked to gender, age, skin color or nationality1). In other words, the aim is to guarantee equal rights, whether for securing a loan, access to public services, hiring ...

### ... and make it strategic

And here's when we need to talk about responsible Al. Let's say that in our first example, you're no longer the one applying for the loan. You're the one who manages the bank or the IT system or the analytics. And for you, "Responsible AI" means "yet more new regulations, more rules to change and implement!". But if we tell you that responsible AI will help you optimize your costs, beef up your customer service or even your loyalty/satisfaction strategy, and easily maintain your platforms while complying with regulations, perhaps you'll see it as a major opportunity to build future-proof practices and business models. Let's rephrase: responsible AI does not have to be synonymous with constraints and compliance. On the contrary: because it is responsible, this approach to AI creates value and gives companies a true competitive edge.

Responsible AI is all the more critical now that generative AIs (see below) have entered with a bang into all strata of society. The biases remain the same as those of the "old" AI. But their effects have multiplied: using colossal volumes of data2 , these "GenAI" generate new data, which is in turn used as input for decision-making. How can we trust them, and guarantee that an organization's products and services are reliable? Responsible AI is therefore becoming a cornerstone of business strategy. And we're not talking here about 5, 10 or 15-year business strategies. We're talking about what can be implemented now, with today's know-how and knowledge. This white paper is a practical guide to responsible AI for business.

\* 1 There are already many examples of algorithmic discriminatory behaviors that led to scandals that have tarnished the reputation and business of large companies. Read: "Apple card investigated after gender discrimination complaints", "Amazon scraps secret Al recruiting tool that showed bias against women", "LAPD will end controversial program that aimed to predict where crimes would occur"

\* 2 Gartner predicts that, within three years, generative AI will produce 10% of all data, i.e. tens of billions of gigabytes. Read: https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2021-10-18-gartner-identifies-the-top-strategic-technology-trends-for-2022

## INTERPRETABILITY, EXPLAINABILITY: WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE?

The interpretability pillar consists in configuring an algorithmic model to allow access to the factors that influence predictions/decisions throughout the Al lifecycle. This work is carried out by a data scientist.

The explainability pillar consists in explaining the results (derived from interpretability) to the users of an Al solution (so that they can understand them and adopt the solution).

It refers to the practice of preserving human involvement and oversight in the decision-making processes of artificial intelligence systems. This involvement ensures accountability and helps prevent potential biases or errors in Al-driven decisions. Moreover, by preserving the fundamental human need for control and agency in decision- making processes, it fosters adoption of the solution.

## · Generative AI for dummies

### Generative AIs create content...

... as if they were you, based on one of your requests. Text, images, video, sound: they magnify human creative processes; it only takes them a few seconds to generate a text (with ChatGPT3) or an image (with Midjourney).

### What is the difference with the "old" AI?

Until now, AIs were based mainly on "structured" data: descriptive, numerical information in spreadsheets (business accounts, temperature measurements for weather forecasts, sales figures, etc.). Generative AIs are based on "unstructured" data (text, images, video, sound); in a way, they create "new" content.

### What challenges to achieve what success?

### Relevance.

How do we control hallucinations and biases while respecting the regulatory framework, in a context with a low acceptable error on decision-making? How do we ensure that the content is contextualized and actionable in a specific sector, business, use and time?

<!-- PageFooter: 3 3 GPT-3 and GPT-4 are LLMs (Large Language Models), which are generative AI algorithms, a Deep Learning method, a subset of Machine Learning, itself a subset of Data Science. page 03 -->
<!-- PageBreak -->

<!-- PageHeader: Ekimetrics. -->

Generative AI's true significance lies in its capacity to address specific problems within well-structured ecosystems. Beyond the hype, it becomes a valuable tool when applying meticulous data preprocessing and interface development to deliver human-readable results, through techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (a technique incorporating the corrections made by annotators to a ranking of answers proposed by the generative AI algorithm. Thanks to RLHF, the algorithm learns to generate responses that would be validated by humans).

>> From a business viewpoint, the goal is to overcome the current pitfalls of AI and LLMs to deliver trustworthy models that exactly and specifically match an organization's strategy and operations.

### Embedding.

How do we embed these complex models in specific IT legacy and activation tools? How can we be sure they match an organization and its processes? How do we combine them with lighter models and human-led decision-making steps?

Integrating Generative AI into an ecosystem mirrors traditional data projects, involving data structuring and user-centric refinement. Its unique strength lies in presenting meaningful outcomes to users, through constant adaptation and incorporation of feedback to enhance its accuracy.

>> In practice, AI needs to be fully integrated and embedded in a company's workflows, processes and systems.

### Control.

How do we control the cost of internalizing such technologies? Beyond the tech component and the training cost, what technical skills are required? How can we trust the security and privacy of these technologies?

Monitoring Generative AI in production poses distinctive challenges compared to traditional algorithms. User feedback and comparisons become pivotal in defining a good model and ensuring long-term effectiveness while mitigating bias. Maintenance efforts are vital to uphold performance quality, and users will play an essential role in adapting to and refining their interactions with Generative AI.

>> Securing access to data requires deploying Responsible AI models by design, compliant with the EU AI Act and developed with weighted models to control for cost and energy consumption.

### 02

#### L'IA responsable

#### L'IA RESPONSABLE

Impact AI propose une définition et un choix de méthodes de mise en œuvre d'une IA responsable. Le collectif répertorie des outils conformes à des valeurs éthiques, les met à disposition de tous et vérifie leur pertinence dans le temps.

##### Qu'est-ce que l'IA responsable ?

C'est une intelligence artificielle conçue pour rester toujours sous le contrôle humain. Elle est fiable et robuste c'est-à-dire qu'elle fait ce qu'elle promet et que son fonctionnement garantit sûreté et sécurité. Elle est aussi respectueuse du droit, du consentement de l'utilisateur, de la vie privée et des libertés fondamentales ; son fonctionnement est explicable et transparent. Au-delà de la responsabilité des utilisateurs de l'IA, cette définition questionne celles des développeurs et des organisations. La conviction d'Impact Al est qu'il faut passer d'un usage responsable à une IA responsable par essence, by design. Au-delà des objectifs louables poursuivis par les services développés, l'intelligence artificielle doit comporter la notion de responsabilité dans son ADN.

Quel est l'enjeu de l'IA responsable ?

Bien que l'intelligence artificielle représente de formidables opportunités pour l'humanité, son rapide développement suscite des craintes. On redoute que ses usages ne contreviennent à des valeurs éthiques (privation de liberté, violations des droits de l'Homme, inégalités de chances ... ) ; on appréhende que sa complexification grandissante n'en fasse perdre le contrôle. Impact Al croit donc que pour créer les conditions de la confiance, il faut avant tout s'assurer que l'humain se trouve toujours au cœur de la conception des systèmes puis prouver que ceux-ci respectent les engagements des entreprises. Analyser et mesurer les impacts directs et indirects de l'IA sur la société est une condition sine qua non pour avancer sur la voie du progrès.

##### Quelles sont les missions que se fixe Impact AI ?

Le collectif veut contribuer à la mise en place d'une IA responsable. Il apporte ses réflexions à l'ensemble de l'écosystème et, dans un esprit d'ouverture et collaboratif, il propose des solutions concrètes qui pourront inspirer les acteurs et les aider à élaborer des politiques éthiques. Des outils de gouvernance et techniques, des formations et des publications sont regroupés dans une boîte à outils en libre accès sur le site d'Impact Al. Sans prétendre à l'exhaustivité, elle s'enrichit au fil du temps.

## 6· Robustness pillar

### Core concept Measure and ensure model performance and stability throughout its lifecycle

#### What are the risks?

· For your business customers > incorrect predictions, obsolete solution

· For your organization > model maintenance problems, additional financial costs, brand image/reputation and business, industrial espionage, sabotage, ethics and compliance issues, non-reactivity to changes

Where do you start?

V Deploying a data architecture designed to check the reliability of the prediction results while continuing to integrate new data.

V Operationalize and standardize continuous model training using model training pipelines (thus avoiding drift)

V Implement observability and monitoring of data and the Al by gathering statistics, performance data and metrics to improve system performance

### What's the competitive advantage?

· For your business customers > trust, adoption

## DATA AND MODEL DRIFTS

- Data drift refers to the phenomenon where the characteristics of the input data that an AI model was trained on, gradually diverge from the characteristics of the data it encounters in a real-world production environment. This can occur due to changes in user behavior, shifts in market trends, or other external factors that influence data distribution over time.

- Model drift refers to the situation where an AI model's performance gradually diminishes over time as the underlying assumptions or conditions in the operational environment change. This can occur due to shifts in user preferences, alterations in the business landscape, or other dynamic factors that impact the relevance of the model.

### GenAIs are expanding into the world of business...

... to win the race against time, cumbersome tasks such as taking minutes at meetings, writing e-mails and summarizing documents can now be performed by generative AIs like ChatGPT. Corollary: employees can refocus their productivity on higher value-added tasks.

Banking4, finance, media, NGOs, ESG players: some sectors are pioneers in the use of these new technologies. In fact, Ekimetrics has already been asked to implement:

Question answering and sourcing: with their ability to search for information in massive databases, new-generation AIs produce immediate answers to business questions, and can isolate specific criteria (a selection of CVs for HR; or in healthcare, in diagnosis tools or looking up information in research literature, for example). The demand for transparency, explainability and security is driving companies to implement a kind of internal ChatGPT, enabling them to track the source of the information they need. #### 3.2.3. Bias and discrimination

Machine-learning models have been the subject of criticism for over a decade because of their vulnerability to data that contain biases or that present a skewed view of reality due to their incompleteness or unrepresentative datasets.349 Al-generated text, images, audio, and video have also been shown to exhibit this same vulnerability. The source of bias in the output of these models can be traced back to biases and misrepresentations that exist in datasets used to train the models. And those flaws in the datasets can often reflect a lack of diversity among key decision-makers in developing and training the models.350

#### 3.2.3.A. Bias in training datasets

Al experts consider training data to be the most salient source of bias in generative Al models. For example, GPT- 2's training data comes from outbound links from Reddit, a social network often criticized for hosting anti-feminist content.351 As a result, Al models trained on such data are more likely to produce outputs that reflect these biases. Biases in training data are likely to "disproportionately align with existing regimes of power."352 For example, prior to the #MeToo movement, the internet was influenced by male-dominated institutions and media that downplayed gender-based violence. Algorithms and content moderation amplified voices aligned with these power structures, giving minimal space to allegations of sexual misconduct. Consequently, Al models trained on pre-#MeToo data absorbed these biases, producing responses downplaying gender-based violence. During

the #MeToo movement, social media platforms and news outlets were filled with content on gender inequality and sexual harassment. So, training data collected during this period likely captured more content reflecting the prevalence of sexual harassment and violence against women.353 Either way, the biases and blindspots of society are scraped into databases for training Al models, and those models conjure up their outputs based on what they have in those databases.

Another problem with datasets used to train large language models can be that they lack representation of languages from groups that are already disproportionately marginalized or excluded. Over 60% of all websites, for instance, are in English. As a result, large language models underperform in non-English languages, resulting in disparities in content for different groups in a global society. Training the same algorithm on datasets of Korean or French texts, for instance, would certainly result in different model outputs. Moreover, large language models may harbor hidden biases based on language. Recent research revealed that certain Al systems exhibit a higher likelihood of recommending the death penalty for a fictional defendant who presents a statement in African American English (AAE)-a dialect spoken by millions in the United States-compared to a statement in Standardized American English (SAE).354 Additionally, the chatbots were more prone to assigning AAE speakers to less prestigious jobs.

The issue of bias is not limited to text-based Al but can also be seen in image-based models. Some synthetic image generation systems overrepresent white skin tones and male features.355 For instance, when researchers evaluated images created by Stable Diffusion against statistics for US demographics for various occupations, they found discrepancies: Although statistics showed that women constitute 39% of doctors, images of women as doctors accounted for only 7% of the images of doctors generated by the Al model. The study established a similar pattern for judges: Women represent 34% of the profession but appear in just 3% of the images of judges.356 More broadly, outputs from generative Al might reflect this pattern of discrimination toward other specific social and religious groups.357
